questions.question: Which statement is a falsifiable chaos-engineering hypothesis?
options: Terminate a checkout instance
Checkout success remains at or above 99% when one replica is terminated
The service uses three replicas
The dashboard should look healthy
questions.explanation: A hypothesis predicts a measurable system output under a named fault. Terminating an instance is only the fault action.

questions.question: Why should the hypothesis boundary differ from the abort boundary?
options: The hypothesis boundary judges the claim, while the abort boundary limits unacceptable impact
The abort boundary is only used after cleanup
The hypothesis boundary grants fault permissions
They must always be the same value
questions.explanation: A hypothesis can be safely falsified before customer impact becomes severe enough to require stopping the experiment.

questions.question: A dependency fault causes 99.2% success, 2.6-second p95 latency, and 132% modeled worker utilization. What is the best conclusion?
options: The system is healthy because success exceeds 99%
The experiment is inconclusive because success is nonzero
The response is unsafe because latency and worker saturation reveal propagation
The fault tool must have failed
questions.explanation: One healthy-looking metric does not override violated latency and capacity guardrails. The local dependency fault has propagated into shared resources.

questions.question: What does a bounded timeout prove by itself?
options: The product continues successfully
The dependency is durable
One attempt cannot occupy the caller beyond the timeout budget
Retries are always safe
questions.explanation: A timeout protects waiting time and capacity. It does not provide a successful fallback, correctness, or independent capacity.

questions.question: Why is immediate retry dangerous during connection resets?
options: It can amplify work against an already failing dependency and consume shared capacity
It automatically opens a circuit breaker
It removes the need for idempotency
It guarantees lower latency
questions.explanation: Unbounded or synchronized retries add work during failure. Backoff, jitter, retry budgets, and idempotency are needed to contain amplification.

questions.question: An experiment finishes its fault action successfully. What must happen before the run is considered complete?
options: Only the tool status needs to be archived
The team must verify cleanup, steady-state recovery, queues, replicas, and delayed side effects
The same fault must immediately run again
All alerts must be disabled
questions.explanation: Removing the injected condition is not proof of recovery. The system and user-visible steady state must be checked after cleanup.

questions.question: When is it reasonable to expand a chaos experiment into production?
options: Before target selection is reviewed
After safeguards, observability, cleanup, ownership, and a small blast radius have been rehearsed
Whenever a production incident is already active
Only when no abort condition exists
questions.explanation: Production adds realism and risk. The team should first prove the experiment's controls and then begin with a short, tightly bounded cohort.
